lesson.menu_desc: Reading about why busy people bake bread on Saturday mornings -- dough, yeast, a crispy loaf -- and describing recipes, people and places: the recipe that..., the baker who..., the kitchen where... -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Weekend Baking
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Caroline Teixeira Nomiyama | Lesson 10 -- Weekend Baking
lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses: who (people), which (things), that (people or things), where (places), whose (possession) -- a loaf whose crust is crispy; the kitchen where I bake

listenings.text: I teach bread classes on Saturday mornings, and the people who come are usually very busy. Lawyers, doctors, teachers. They arrive tired, and they look at their phones all the time. Then I give them flour, water, salt and yeast, and I ask them to knead the dough for ten minutes. Something changes. They stop talking about work. After that, we wait for the dough to rise, and that is the part which surprises them most. They want to do something, but bread needs time. When the loaves come out of the oven, everybody is smiling. Most of them say the same thing: it was the first quiet morning they had in months.

My grandmother was a woman whose bread was famous in our little town. Every Sunday, people came to her house to buy a loaf. When she died, I found her recipe in an old notebook. It was very short: four ingredients and three lines. So I tried it. My first loaf was a disaster. It didn't rise, and it was as hard as a rock. My second one was better, but the crust wasn't crispy. I baked every weekend for a year. Now I make bread that tastes almost like hers. Almost. I think the secret is the oven. Hers was a big old one, which she used for everything.

The first time I tried Brazilian cheese bread was in a small cafe in New York, where a Brazilian couple worked. I thought it was just bread, but it was different. It was crispy outside, and soft and a little chewy inside. I asked the owner for the recipe, and she laughed. Then she explained that there is no wheat flour and no yeast in it. They use a flour which comes from cassava, a root. And you don't knead it like normal dough. Today I make it at home on Sundays, for friends who visit me. It's the recipe that people always ask me for.

reading.rtitle: Weekend Baking: Why Bread Is Worth the Wait
paras: On weekdays, most of us eat bread that comes from a supermarket. It is soft, it is cheap, and it lasts for a week. But more and more people who work long hours are spending their Saturday mornings in the kitchen, with their hands in a bowl of dough. Why? Home bakers say the answer is simple: bread is one of the few things in life that you cannot rush.

A basic loaf needs only four ingredients: flour, water, salt and yeast. Yeast is the small living thing which makes the dough rise. First, you mix everything and knead the dough for about ten minutes, until it is smooth. Then you wait. The dough needs one or two hours in a warm place where it can rise and double in size. Finally, you bake it in a very hot oven. The result is a loaf whose crust is crispy and whose inside is soft and light.

Many home bakers say that the waiting is the best part. A London baker who teaches weekend classes says that her students arrive stressed and leave calm. "Kneading is good for the mind," she says. "You can't check your phone when your hands are covered in flour." And you don't need to be an expert. Find a simple recipe, follow it step by step, and don't worry if your first loaf isn't perfect. The second one will be better.
